chunks.content: 96 Purchase Agreements: Your (Not-So-Boring) Deal Survival Guide Hi Sara, If you're buying an accounting firm, you’re going to meet a purchase agreement. And by “meet,” I mean it’s going to sit on your desk like a 40-page foreign language exam. Let’s change that. Purchase agreements can look intimidating, but under all that legal lingo, there’s a pattern. A structure. Dare I say... a method to the madness. And understanding it can save you from signing something that quietly sets your hair on fire. Here’s the cheat sheet I share with clients: Article 1: What You’re Actually Buying Assets, price, terms. It's all in here. Read it like your career depends on it (because it might). Bonus tip: Make sure you understand what's excluded, not just what you're getting. Because if it’s not listed clearly, you’re probably not getting it. Article 3: The Great List of Promises These are the seller’s (and your) reps and warranties. Think of this as the “are you telling the truth and nothing but the truth?” section. The hidden magic? These reps force sellers to disclose things they “forgot” to mention—like pending lawsuits or unpaid wage claims. That’s not just legal housekeeping. That’s gold. Article 5: Covenants, aka The Thou Shalt Nots This is where the non-competes, non-solicits, and general behavior clauses live. Are they enforceable? Reasonable? Clear enough that you won’t accidentally trip over them just by breathing in the wrong ZIP code? Let’s hope so. Article 6: Indemnification Also known as “who’s cleaning up the mess if something goes wrong?” This section matters a lot more than people think, especially when a third party crashes the party with a lawsuit. Miscellaneous: The Sneaky Stuff Boilerplate doesn’t mean unimportant. I’ve found all kinds of landmines hiding in those standard-seeming sections. Read them. All of them. Yes, even the severability clause. Signature Lines: Who’s Actually on the Hook Make sure individuals are signing, not just LLCs. You can’t hold “ABC Accounting, LLC” accountable when it vanishes six months after closing. You want Jim Anderson’s signature if Jim Anderson is the one making promises. Still awake? Then you, my friend, are the exact kind of person I want reading these emails. If this made the fog of legalese lift even a little, and you're thinking “Hey, maybe I don’t need to go to law school after all,” you’re welcome. But if you want to dig even deeper without the student debt, check out Deal Academy or subscribe to my YouTube channel for more plain-English tips on deal-making done right.
